item.title: Every Body: Sexuality Doesn’t End at 50
item.description:
Sex

Every Body: Sexuality Doesn’t End at 50

Women over 50 are redefining desire, pleasure, dating, and sexual freedom.

Posted September 4, 2026

Key points
  • Sexual ageism is the assumption that sexuality, desire, and pleasure naturally belong to the young.
  • Sexuality in midlife isn't necessarily about trying to preserve the sex life someone had when she was younger.
  • Research and women's experiences show us just how varied sexuality can remain throughout our lives.

Every September 4th, World Sexual Health Day is celebrated and brings attention to sexual health, bodily rights, pleasure, and well-being around the globe. This year’s theme, “EVERY BODY,” offers an opportunity to explore sexuality for all bodies, including those people over 50.

The stereotype that sexual desire and pleasure belong primarily to younger bodies is particularly strong for women. As women move through midlife, they are often viewed as less sexually desirable, or even asexual. Yet current research tells a much different story. Women over 50 continue to have sex, masturbate, orgasm, date, and seek intimacy and pleasure.

Sexual Ageism: When Older Bodies Stop Being Seen as Sexual

Source: Pexels/VladaKarpovich

Sexual ageism is the assumption that sexuality, desire, and pleasure naturally belong to the young. A 2026 review published in Sexual Medicine Reviews, Luria et al. describes how these attitudes can show up in media, healthcare, younger generations, and even in the way people come to view their own sexuality as they age. The authors note that media often portray people later in life as either asexual or hypersexual, while continuing to emphasize youthfulness as the standard of sexual desirability.

For women, there is another layer. The researchers discuss a “double standard of aging,” in which men can remain sexually desirable (grey foxes) as they get older while women are more likely to be viewed as sexually undesirable because of their age, changing bodies and/or greying hair. These messages obviously matter because all people internalize them, which impacts how women feel about freely expressing their own sexuality and desires.

Sexuality After 50: What Are Women Actually Doing?

A 2022 University of Michigan National Poll on Healthy Aging asked women ages 50–80 about sex and intimacy. Two in five women ages 50–80 (43%) said they had been sexually active in the past year, such as caressing, foreplay, masturbation, or intercourse. Among women ages 50–64, that number rose to 53%. Interestingly, nearly two-thirds (62%) of women said they were satisfied with their sexual activity.

Source: Pexels/cottonbrostudio

A more recent 2025 study published in Menopause gives us an even closer look at sexual pleasure in midlife. Graham et al., surveyed 1,500 U.S. women ages 40–65, with an average age of 52.5, about masturbation and orgasm. More than half had masturbated within the previous year. Among the women who masturbated, they reported reaching orgasm an average of 81% of the time.

The researchers also asked women to think about how the quality of their orgasms had changed over the previous 10 years. More women reported that their orgasms had gotten better rather than worse, although most said they had stayed the same.

These findings don't mean that sexuality stays exactly the same as women age. Menopause, health, relationships, and changing bodies can all influence sexuality. But turning 50 alone tells us very little about whether a woman is interested in sex or pleasure.

A Different Kind of Sexual Freedom

Source: Pexels/cottonbrostudio

Sexuality in midlife also isn't necessarily about trying to preserve the sex life someone had when she was younger. For some women, this stage of life can bring an entirely different relationship with sex.

In 2023, researchers Luke and Poulin in the Journal of Family Theory & Review reviewed 11 studies examining the sexual experiences of single women in midlife. One of the studies followed 16 American women aged 57–91, most of whom had entered new sexual relationships after divorce. Many described enjoying the energy and passion of these new relationships and exploring their sexuality in a new way. They found themselves becoming better at knowing and asking for what they wanted from sexual partners.

Dating After 50: “We Can Choose What We Want”

Many women who come into sex therapy at midlife report that they are looking to not only address their biomedical symptoms of menopause, but also to seek a deeper relationship with their own desires. When asked what their desires are at this time, many of them say they never really asked themselves what they wanted and spent most of their partnered years focusing on their partner’s desires. What women begin to learn through their sex therapy experiences is what they want, how to ask for the kind of sexuality that is most erotic and pleasurable for them and what to do when their partner might push back on their requests.

Source: Pexels/RonLach

Whether midlife women are partnered in a monogamous relationship, single and dating, or in consensually non-monogamous relationships, most midlife women come to own their desires and discover they’re embarking on a new and exciting new journey.

There can be something freeing about that. After decades of being told what a relationship or sex life is supposed to look like, learning sex esteem frameworks offer women more permission to ask a much simpler question: What do I actually want?

What We're Starting to See on Screen

We may finally be starting to see some of that freedom reflected on screen too.

Source: imdb.com

In the 2026 film I Want Your Sex, Olivia Wilde plays Erika Tracy, a sexually confident older artist who begins a Dom/sub relationship with her younger assistant. The film was co-written by longtime sex writer Karley Sciortino, who interviewed this author years ago for her VICE show Slutever on the orgasm gap between men and heterosexual women.

About her own history growing up, Sciortino puts the double standard particularly well:

“As a millennial, I was raised on the idea that a woman’s expiration date was basically 40, while at 45, George Clooney was the most eligible bachelor alive.”

She writes that female desire has been put on the back burner for the longest time, so seeing it show up loudly on screen can feel like a win. As she puts it: “Gen X and older millennial women are aging into midlife and saying, “No, actually, I’m not doing the invisible thing.”

Every Body Means Every Age

None of this means that every woman over 50 wants sex or should. That would simply replace one stereotype with another.

Source: Pexels/RDNEStockproject

Instead, the research and women's experiences show us just how varied sexuality can remain throughout our lives. Women over 50 are having sex, masturbating, orgasming, dating, entering new relationships, exploring what they want, and sometimes redefining what sex and intimacy mean to them.

This World Sexual Health Day, “Every Body” gives us an opportunity to explore all sexuality, including that of more mature women. Our bodies may change as we age. What we want may change too. But neither desire nor pleasure comes with an expiration date.

item.title: Will More Arguments Make You More Persuasive? It Depends
item.description:
Persuasion

Will More Arguments Make You More Persuasive? It Depends

Consider your audience during persuasion attempts.

Posted September 4, 2026

Key points
  • Presenting more arguments in a persuasion attempt leads to perceptions that the persuader has expertise.
  • Presenting more arguments can also lead the target to believe the persuader has ulterior motives.
  • The implication is that the situation and the target govern when to use more or fewer persuasive arguments.

You are trying to convince someone — your friend, a client, your spouse — to take some action or change their belief, and you have lots of supporting arguments to make. Should you simply pile on all of the arguments in favor of your position? Or, would the other person think that you were “trying too hard” and be turned off by all of your arguments?

More traditional research suggests that having more arguments makes you more persuasive. A very recent study, however, suggests that it’s more complicated than that. While using more arguments in a persuasion attempt may make you look more like an expert, presenting a lot of arguments may also make the target person skeptical about your intentions. They may wonder, does this person have ulterior motives and is just trying to “sell” me on this?

A series of recent studies (Bergman et al., 2025) explored these factors and has contested the general belief that more arguments are more persuasive. In these experiments, people were given varying numbers of arguments (1, 3, 6, or 9 supporting arguments) from a persuasive individual, and then measures were taken of whether they were actually persuaded.

While more arguments did lead to perceptions that the persuader had more expertise, it also increased people’s skepticism and concern that the persuader had ulterior motives, or what the researchers termed “persuasive intent.”

The bottom line is this: If you are trying to be persuasive, you need to consider the other person — the target of your persuasion attempt — and that person’s perspective. Is the person focused on determining if you have expertise (that you actually know what you are arguing for, and you have supporting evidence/arguments), or are they wary that you have ulterior motives in your persuasion attempt? That should affect the number (and type) of arguments you present. As the researchers conclude, their results suggest “that situational constraints can dictate when it is better to advocate using more or fewer arguments.”

In another interesting study (Wallace, et al., 2024), researchers found that persons who are members of disadvantaged groups who are arguing for their rights can be seen as informed “experts” on the issue (e.g., discrimination against the disadvantaged group), but they also may be less persuasive if their targeted audience views them as having a vested interest (i.e., when, borrowing liberally from William Shakespeare, the persuader “doth argue too much”).

Again, it depends on who is being persuaded. The researchers, in summary, say: “When expertise is prioritized, providing more arguments is more persuasive, but when persuasive intent is prioritized, providing fewer arguments might be a better strategy.”

item.title: You Have Already Died: Jung's Rebirth Archetype
item.description:
Identity

You Have Already Died: Jung's Rebirth Archetype

The psyche rehearses death long before we understand what it's preparing us for.

Posted September 4, 2026

Key points
  • Psychological development is not merely the accumulation of more skills or knowledge.
  • Death and rebirth are archetypally woven into psychological development.
  • Becoming ourselves requires letting parts of ourselves die.
Source: Photo by Pretty Pink on Unsplash

Many of us spend years trying to acquire the right career, friends, hobbies, interests, romantic partner(s), and even a highly specific coffee order. Then, rather inconveniently, something within us stops wanting any of it. Suddenly, relationships sever, the job feels wrong, our interests change, and the old ambitions have become strangely outdated. Even our half sugar, no whip, pumpkin spice latte made with oat milk seems to belong to someone else we no longer recognize.

In these situations, we can witness how death is psychologically present long before biological death arrives within our lifespan.

Carl Jung, the pioneering founder of analytical psychology, was fascinated by the persistent appearance of death and rebirth imagery throughout mythology, religion, dreams, ritual, art, culture, and inner life.1 What interested him was what this persistent imagery implied about our own psychology; that the psyche possesses its own transformative intelligence, and that this intelligence is oriented toward a centre other than the rational mind, or what can be referred to as our small ‘i’ (ego). Jung named that centre of the human psyche the Self.

The negotiation between the egoic rational mind and the Self is where the death and rebirth motif lives for most of us.

Psychological Deaths

We typically experience many symbolic, intangible, and psychological deaths throughout our ordinary lives. As adults, our childhood eventually disappears, an identity that once organized our life stops fitting for whatever reason, and we may lose ways of relating that existed inside a particular community or familial role.

Sometimes these symbolic deaths can be chosen, but for most of us, they often arrive without our consent. I don’t think it’s a stretch to say that most of us have both mercifully and tragically outlived certain fashion trends; the point here being that there are moments in life when something that once gave our lives structure simply no longer does. So, what ends is a structure of identification.

Jungian analysts and depth psychotherapists often describe human development as a psychological process where our ego is periodically dismantled and reconstituted to something larger, and to something it does not author. In other words, life transitions often feel larger than their presenting circumstances; a job ending, for example, is often an initiation into not knowing one’s own identity or worth in Western society.

I also find the language we use for these transitions to be illuminating, as it is common to hear people describe this process as letting go, shedding an old self, being reborn, starting over, losing oneself, or becoming someone new. These statements precisely capture the death and rebirth archetype that Jung was referring to.

The Space In-Between

My colleague and I previously wrote about how past cultures have taken this archetypal pattern seriously, and how other human civilizations successfully built containers for these types of threshold experiences.2 These in-between times are so structurally ambiguous, where people are no longer who they once were, and they are not yet what they will be.

In our modern era, we have continued to experience these life transitions like our ancestors, but now many of us no longer have the support we need for these liminal times. Many experience psychological death-and-rebirth periods with no name, and often within communities that only see them as problems to be immediately corrected or rationally solved.

Interestingly enough, Stanislav and Christina Grof made this the centre of their clinical argument within the field of transpersonal psychology: Episodes of psycho-spiritual transformation are frequently met as pathology alone within many clinical spaces, and it’s often because the clinician lacks a framework in which a person coming apart might also be a person who is being reorganized at a deeper level.3 If we only see distress through a lens of deficit, then the meaning of the distress can easily be lost.

Psychological Rebirth

Jung's writings highlight how rebirth is not simply restoration, but a process of renewal through which the psyche is fundamentally changed.1

Source: Photo by Art Institute of Chicago on Unsplash; Orpheus Playing the Lyre to Hades and Persephone

The myth of Persephone offers a striking image of this transformation, as her descent into the underworld is not chosen; she is abducted and taken there against her will. After eating the pomegranate seeds, she cannot simply return to the life she knew before, and she must return to the world above while remaining bound, in some sense, to the world below. Persephone embodies the tension of psychological transformation itself: descent and return; loss and renewal; the self we were and the self that emerges.

This provides us with an image of psychological development that is very different from simply acquiring more coping tools or trying to recover who we were before a period of significant change. Persephone reminds us that it is the experience of the descent itself that changes us, and that transformation may require us to hold the tension between what has ended and what is emerging, rather than try to resolve it too quickly.

It is also imperative to recognize how emotionally distressing and profoundly uncomfortable it is to enter the stretch of time between a psychological death and rebirth. As a result, many of us want to quickly convert our ending into a new beginning, as there is no glamour, praise, fun, or ease in not knowing who we are becoming. Yet, I have found in my clinical work that the psychological task here is often to resist immediately filling the void, and to actively grieve what has psychologically died.

Returning to Self

In the middle of these difficult life passages, people in my consulting room have often reported something interesting: a unique type of awareness that persists while an old identity dissolves and dies. To me, this illuminates how our rational minds are clearly not the whole of us, and that it is truly possible for us to survive an aspect of our ego dying.

I think it’s fair to say we often encounter endings long before we fully understand what they are preparing us for.

item.title: The Rewards Of Learning to do What’s Difficult
item.description:
Education

The Rewards Of Learning to do What’s Difficult

Mastering life’s challenges are less about skills and more about emotions.

Posted September 4, 2026

Key points
  • Challenges are tied to facing something new, but what gets in the way is the feeling that it is difficult.
  • Overall learning to do what seems difficult is a life long skill that builds self-confidence and self-esteem.
  • The keys are settling goals, having realistic expectations, taking baby-steps, experimenting.
Source: geralt/pixabay

Life is filled with challenges, but often what turns an event or situation into a challenge is that it is new. It requires learning new skills and doing something you’ve never done before, whether it’s learning multiplication tables in the third grade, confronting your supervisor about your work schedule, or fixing a leaking faucet in your bathroom. It’s easy to feel overwhelmed, unsure how to start, already anticipating a negative outcome, or even feeling victimized by life, all of which can stop you in your tracks.

For many, the feeling that it’s all too difficult—not the learning itself—is the real culprit that keeps you from putting the challenge to rest. Rather than learning to override these negative feelings, you take the easier path—put up with the schedule or quit the job, let the faucet drip.

But it’s not just the faucet or the job; this struggle to do what seems difficult can easily become a modus operandi, the way you handle most challenges. Why? Because it works, at least for a while. But over time, it can take its toll in two ways:

Problems pile up.

Unsolved problems are like piles of newspapers you never throw out, cluttering your everyday life. You may learn to navigate around them, but over time, your emotional and mental space shrinks, and the quality of your life becomes the sum of what you avoid.

Your self-esteem and self-image take a hit.

Living this way, it’s easy to come to see yourself as a loser, a victim, or both. You miss the ego boost and self-confidence that come only from tackling challenges, facing your initial fears, and coming out the other side intact. By approaching the anxiety of doing what’s difficult, you learn not only to better tolerate anxiety but also to find that you are more capable and that the world is less scary than you thought. Here’s how to start:

Set out your challenges.

What can’t you do? What is your Achilles’ heel? You have social anxiety that keeps you from socializing; you avoid the plumbing challenge because you long ago decided you have no manual dexterity; because you fear confrontation, you avoid not only confronting your supervisor but also your partner about things that bother you, and instead hold in your complaints and are over-responsible. Decide on one thing that you’d like to conquer.

Set a one-week challenge.

Baby-step time. What is the one thing you can do in the next week to approach rather than avoid your social anxiety, fear of confrontation, or lack of handyman skills? Think behavior, think specific: going out for a beer with a work colleague, letting your partner know you’d like them to put their coffee cup in the dishwasher, or watching YouTube videos on faucet repair. The content doesn’t matter; it’s about going against your grain and doing what you’ve tended to avoid.

Be careful of self-saboteurs.

If you tend to be self-critical or perfectionistic, it can slow you down or stop you. You dawdle about asking your colleague or partner to go out because you’re afraid of doing it wrong; you’re always anticipating it won’t go well. Or you scroll through 30 YouTube videos because you need to find the best one. Maybe you need to be mindful of pacing: you can get impatient and want to do too much too fast.

Good to know, what to do and what not to do. Don’t get bogged down. Move forward. (And add self-criticism to your Achilles’ heel list to tackle later.) Push back against those scolding demons. Slow down and take smaller steps.

Assess.

After your week, step back and assess. But first, pat yourself on the back for taking the risk. Next, for anything you need to tweak or move forward on: Suggest to your colleague going out sooner rather than later; thank your partner for following through; go to the hardware store and get the tools you need.

Keep experimenting.

This suggestion is actually two: The key to learning to do what is difficult is practice, challenging yourself daily and weekly, and learning to approach the difficult so you can better handle problems, learn new skills, feel less anxious, and build your self-confidence and self-esteem.

But the other is about attitude—experimenting. Avoid any impulse to do the makeover; go on the finally-shape-up-stop-put-to-rest campaign. They never work because you run out of gas or take steps that are too big. Instead, be curious, try something new, see what happens, and tweak.

Learning, whether it is about skills, your emotions, or how you think about yourself and the world, is about small steps.

Slow and steady wins the race.
